strings.JAM_paternalism_party_long: Jamaica Labour Party - Bustamante Industrial Trade Union
strings.JAM_front_long: People's Freedom Movement - People's National Party
strings.JAM_committee_long: Committee of the Jamaican United Front
strings.JAM_political_violence_desc:
There are two parties in Jamaica that truly matter. One one side is the social-democratic People's National Party; on the other is the conservative Jamaica Labour Party. These two factions, longtime rivals, have engaged in many political battles before, but another facet of Jamaican politics is left off official records - not back-room deals, but back-alley shootings, which have only become more common in the politically tense times we live in.

Each day, youth gangs take to the streets clad in the colors of their favored party, ready to agitate their rivals, packing lead pipes, knives, and pistols to use. Jamaican side streets are the scenes of brawls, flurries of violence that break apart with the crack of guns and the shouts of police. The murder rate has skyrocketed, and the violence shows no sign of abating, despite the efforts of both parties to disavow their violent supporters. It seems only calmer times will fix this bloody rupture - or, at least, return it to its normal rate.
strings.JAM_miracle_desc:
While the world has spiraled further and further in chaos and conflict, these interesting times seem to have spared Jamaica from its worst effects. Indeed, a major reason of our secession from the Federation goes back to the sudden success of our economy - an economy that is now for Jamaica's benefit, and Jamaica alone.

Never before have the people enjoyed such wealth as they do now, as trade rolls in from the United States and the other Caribbean nations and tourists flock to our golden beaches and clear blue skies. The wealth of our island, both in appearance and in resources, spurs our economic growth to greater and greater heights. As the money rolls in, we can raise a glass to prosperity, and relax secure in the knowledge that Jamaica has never been more free or wealthy than it is today.
strings.JAM_rastafarian_repression_desc:
Jamaican culture is inexorably tied to the Rastafarians. Born in the impoverished Black communities of the early 20th century, this unique religion has been the cause of interest for decades, with their worship of Emperor Haile Selassie as the messiah, smoking of “ganja”, and distinctive dialect. These worshippers used to be little more than a curious subculture, keeping to themselves and meeting peacefully to spread their beliefs - but the Rastafari have grown far beyond their humble roots.

The relationship between the religion and the government has always been strained, with the believers seeing non-believers as instruments of the decadent Babylon and non-believers seeing believers as delusional, but recent events have only amplified that tense relationship. Many believed that the exiled Selassie, being the Messiah, would never die, and his death has splintered parts of the Rastafari into vengeful, aggressive sects with differing explanations on what happened - from postulating that he was only an incarnation of Jah to claiming that Selassie faked his death and now orchestrates massive anti-Italian resistance. These offshoots regularly clash with the overworked police, who increasingly crack down on all Rastafarians, regardless of their personal actions. This spiral only worsens with every incident, and neither side has any trust or love lost for the other.

If a solution is not found, tensions could boil over in a deadly way.
strings.JAM_jamaica_first_desc:
First, it was the Spanish. They arrived hundreds of years ago in their massive warships, bringing deadly disease, cannons, and slaves. Taíno and escaped slaves held out in the hills, escaping and resisting their clutches - the first native Jamaican identity emerging from their fight.

Then it was the British, who replaced the Spanish in name but no less in cruelty. Plantations sprung up, along with thousands upon thousands of settlers and slaves, expanding the island massively in population. Still, the Jamaican identity held out in the overlooked nooks and crannies, growing in the places the British did not go.

Time passed. The British loosened their grip, ended slavery on the island, passed more reforms - and then, like a storm, they were swept away in the chaos of the Second World War, and the Americans swooped in to replace them. Jamaica was roped into an ungainly, dysfunctional Federation, designed to take the wealth from Jamaicans and bundle it away. Once again, Jamaica rejected this imperialist dream, and broke free of its repression in spectacular fashion.

Now, Jamaica is free. There are no more empires left to beat back. After centuries of struggle, the Rock will chart its own course and plan its own destiny.

Is there anything sweeter than the taste of freedom?
strings.JAM_Busta_Backbone_desc:
Populism alongside exploitative optimism had transformed Alexander Bustamante's Jamaica Labour Party into an empire of relentless dominance and command, a hegemony permeating into the livelihoods of the everyman as his self-styled “Bustamante Industrial Trade Union” effectively placed much of the nation's working sectors into one authoritarian grasp — a tolerated, if ultimately nasty, piece of reality.

The influence of his machine festers, swelling as few final remnants of the dysfunctional colonial administration seek a willing host with what influence they have left — and more often than not, they'd found Busta obliging to their demands so long as he's compensated fair and upfront. Carrots with sticks had worked for the last few decades, and its enforcer finds it much too beneficial for change.
strings.JAM_Reform_Failures_desc:
Following a series of post-war riots, the US and its colonial allies sought to implement a bold plan of reforms to foster development and bring the islands into the 20th century. Through mismanagement, corruption, and underfunding, the results have been mixed to say the least, but in few places did the schemes go so disastrously as in Jamaica.

The wealth gap continues to rocket, dominance of the white and creole elites solidifies, and the island remains riddled with poverty and crime. All the while, political divisions are growing more extreme, and atop it all, the JLP keeps throwing logs onto the fire.

Once the jewel of the English Caribbean, Jamaica now stands as a testament to the post-war order's failure to truly promote development in the region.
strings.JAM_Kingston_Renaissance_desc:
Inspired by a motley of cultural movements, from the French-imported Négritude to homegrown products such as Garveyism, the streets of Kingston are undergoing a renaissance, motivated by both growing Caribbean nationalism and the emergence of a domestic intellectual class, which has gradually reformed as the Anglos continue loosening their grasp on the last scraps of colonial holdings.

Labor unions and political organizations increasingly attach themselves to the nascent Afro-Caribbean label as identitarian movements such as Rastafarianism gain traction amongst the masses, garnering attention from notables both home and across the pond, whether positively or not. While Kingston continues to be plagued by post-colonial poverty, it has nonetheless made itself, despite everything, a cultural heavyweight — or as some generously call it, the Mecca of Afro-Caribbean culture.
strings.JAM_Posses_Gather_desc:
Across Kingston, gangs now exert their authority. With Jamaica heavily destabilized by the wave of demonstrations against Bustamante. Gang violence has become commonplace, as have its subsequent consequences. Crime of all forms is rampant and regularly targeted at civilians, weapons are freely available, and minimal drug control exists. On paper, legal authority still exists, but it goes no farther than the paper the documents are written upon.

Instead, the real role of governance is to shuffle money across a handful of departments, either to the police in areas they still control or as bribes to gangs momentarily aligned with the government and willing to fight. In time, these donations may shift, but gang warfare will remain a common and widespread issue. As long as this system continues, though, the only people to lose will be Jamaican civilians.
strings.JAM_The_Tropical_Fabian_desc:
The Second World War has not eaten away at the influence that British labour politics holds. With Michael Manley lifted to power in Kingston, he and the People's National Party will push Jamaican politics in the direction of the old Fabian Society. Focused on ensuring the survival of democratic apparati and moderation compared to other factions in the Jamaican Popular Republic, Kingston will follow a Democratic Socialist vision.

Influenced by the developmentalism of the Mexican PRI and of Fidel Castro, Manley will place high attention on building civic apparati aimed at alleviating poverty, improving education, and building infrastructure. Funding for this will also come through increased spending and tariffs, targeted towards large expansions to tourism and bauxite, both industries that already have significant sway within the Jamaican economy and interest from global corporations.
strings.JAM_The_New_Machine_desc:
In attempting to supplant the influence of the Jamaica Labour Party, the People's National Party has had to move beyond the ideals it once held for itself. Figures within the PNP and their relatives have been appointed to key institutional posts, labour unions have been given major strangleholds, and Brigadista radicals work to intimidate opponents into voting for them, or into standing down mid-election.

In some respects, this has worked. The JLP has lost the hold it once had across the country, and is increasingly an empty vessel. But to the average Jamaican, the consequences of this plan working merely echoes the consequences of Bustamante's past plan to prosper. Through the lofty rhetoric and goals claimed by Manley, many Jamaicans simply see the iron fist that once repressed them merely cloaked in a velvet glove.
strings.JAM_Black_Star_Red_Flag_desc:
Jamaica's new ruling government does not have strong cohesion. Formed by Billy Strachan, leader of the Caribbean Legion's Black Star Brigade and a long opponent to the former regime, his government is an eclectic mix of Bolsheviks, black nationalists, moderate socialists and whatever miscellaneous figures have been able to integrate into its officer corps, each now vying for their own influence within the revolutionary government.

In an effort to paper over these cracks, the forces of Billy Strachan largely rule via decree. Fears of surviving loyalists to Bustamante or an intervention from Washington have brought room for emergency measures to be justified, with fervour quickly being melded into mobilization and with the democratic constitution officially suspended. Whatever reaction may arise, Kingston's government will be ready to react in turn.
strings.JAM_The_Maroons_Return_desc:
While our oppressors told themselves that they had ended slavery, they had done no such thing. The plantation economy persisted, Jamaicans forced into exploitation just to survive, and it is only with our triumph that such barbarity has been driven out. We have carried the torch of the Maroon slave revolts, finally eradicated the tools of slavery and white supremacy.

But the struggle cannot end there. A new economy must be formed in the image of those slave revolts of old that fought against the British. Nationalisations and state oversight must permeate, even dominate the economy to ensure injustice is destroyed as quickly as it appears. Yes, businesses are fleeing and the economy is descending into chaos, but that is merely the seed for change. As Strachan says, “change never comes without pain”.
strings.JAM_Revolutionary_Democracy_desc:
Democracy is the fruit of the people, and Jamaica can finally enjoy its true flavor. All eligible citizens shall be free to vote however they wish, unless they seek to subvert this liberation through groups like the JLP. Due to the youth of our newly liberated state however, a popular front has been formed under the tutelage of the Communist People's National Movement, in order to properly form this new democracy.

Tensions remain however. Many social democrats hesitate upon the aggressive revolutions of the front, while traditional labour stalwarts such as Michael Manley look upon our Marxist influences with suspicion and advocate for the reactionary-tainted anglo unionism of before. Such friction threatens our liberation's unity, not to mention the quality of its tutelage. The question of how to resolve such tensions hangs over every party within the front, and it must be answered.
strings.JAM_The_Independence_Debt_desc:
That oppressors fear those who gain the strength to defy them is a universal truth, as true now as it was during the Haitian slave revolts. They will conspire to blockade those brave few and starve them, as they conspired with Haiti. And so, like Haiti, we shall accede to some concessions in the interests of the greater good of the revolution.

This limits the scope of the nationalisations and economic reforms that can be carried out. Foreign businessmen may continue walking our streets, albeit few in number, making a mockery of our social revolution. Few doubt the necessity of such measures in the short term, after all they shall sell us the means to defy them yet further and our new economy remains young and weak. However, how long such concessions can be tolerated remains a contentious question.
strings.JAM_Den_of_Thieves_desc:
Over 250 years ago, the Caribbean was known as a den of crime and vice, where pirates looted and pillaged freely. With Iberia's return to Jamaica as Bustamante's backers, Europeans once again treat the Caribbean as a lawless playground.

Corruption and smuggling have become integral to the Jamaican economy. Funds from illegal weapons and narcotics sales fill the coffers of gang leaders, government officials, and Iberian crimelords alike. European tourists flock to the island, enjoying the sparkling waters of the Caribbean in closed-off resorts, while their countrymen exploit and terrorize the local population in slums just outside the walls. The iron fist and velvet glove of America has disappeared from the island, and in its place, European imperialism returns in its most primal form.
strings.JAM_Bent_Backbone_desc:
The mask has fallen from the Jamaican machine. The regime has turned to outright repression, as state-backed gangs and Iberian mercenaries are used to suppress any and all dissent. Corruption flourishes in plain view, and crime is not just ignored but endorsed, as long as it serves the parties' will. The old system of patronage networks and union coercion has evolved, and the corrupt dictatorship of the JLP dominates for all the world to see.

The man behind it all, Alexander Bustamante, rules over a country bending to his every word, through bribery and violence. Yet his time grows short, and whispers behind his back speculate on his impending death. Party functionaries carve out pieces of Bustamante's empire, as the crooked regime shambles yet forward.
strings.JAM_The_Seaga_Spine_desc:
Edward Seaga ascends to the Premiership in a difficult time. His narrow victory leaves him tied to much of his predecessor's legacy, and massive opposition in both the streets and halls of government leaves his hands tied in many important affairs. Some even predict that his fall is not a matter of if, but when.

But Seaga is no quitter. Patronage networks and state-backed paramilitary gangs are used to consolidate his control, tactics learned from his once-mentor Bustamante. Seaga aims to hold on to power no matter the cost, and digs his claws deeper into the state every day. If the political situation ever reaches a boiling point, Seaga has ensured that he will not be going down without a fight.
strings.JAM_Sunrise_Over_Montego_Bay_desc:
Edward Seaga is painting a new face over Jamaica. Gone are the days of regulations. Gone are the days of labor. The Jamaica of today is a Jamaica open for American tourism. Corruption and crime are shuffled out of view, replaced by billboards and advertisements soliciting investment into new industries on the island.

Nowhere is this more clear than in the city of Montego Bay, where American investments build resorts all across the coastline and fund massive urban redevelopment campaigns. With the backing of American entrepreneurs, Seaga aims to turn Montego Bay into not just a hotspot of tourism, but a model city to represent Jamaica on the world stage, glossing over the criminal underbelly at the heart of the JLP.
strings.JAM_Kingston_Riots_Started_tt: With fires raging across Kingston, an opportunity presents itself...
strings.JAM_flavor.1.desc:
Alexander Bustamante stands with conviction, as the umbras of the Headquarters House looming over him and his cabinet slowly recede. The damages caused by the riots left Jamaica with a shoestring budget. Many expect Bustamante to announce assistance from the OFN to mitigate the damages caused by the riots. Bustamante's printed speech will leave these rumors unfounded.

“The independent committee had carried out a thorough investigation into those responsible for the fatal tragedies in our society, and our findings have uncovered a blatant attempt and betrayal of our autonomy!” His hallmark lofty and emphatic tone was there; somehow, an ominous undertone was also present. “We concluded that these groups of interest were indeed wholly supported, supplied, and contacted by foreign forces, mainly the intelligence departments from the United States of America.”

As CBS telecasts the monumental speech by Bustamante to millions of homes in the United States, the on-site reporter only blanched when Bustamante made the shocking accusation that his most reliable ally would attempt to usurp him, when the embers from the riots were barely snuffed out. No commentary was required to understand the gravity of his upcoming declaration.

“Jamaicans should not have every facet of their society further dictated by malevolent strangers from abroad, neither by America nor Britain. We must take the unfortunate step of separating from British control and chart our own paths forward by declaring independence as a republic, without pause or delay!” The hue and cry quickly masked the few cheers from the audience. “To preserve our sovereignty, we must withdraw our attendance from the negotiations of the West Indies Federation!”

As the situation has not calmed down from the protests of the audience, a photojournalist in the fray has captured his photogenic moment:
strings.JAM_flavor.1.a: Bustamante in the sunlight, his cabinet in the shadows.
strings.JAM_flavor.4.desc:
Canadians, Americans, and British. The delegates belonged to the now-defunct West Indies Commission, somberly traipsed towards the planes that made a one-way trip back to their home countries. To the Iberian ambassador to Jamaica, it paints a small smile on his face to see them fly away, possibly never to come back.

Bustamante's flagrant speech made headlines in both America and Iberia, not just for the sudden turn in foreign policy, but for the Jamaican delegation making headlong advances towards the Iberian Union. The Iberian ambassador, in return, was to make an attendance for the conference for the signing of the new constitution.

The whole charade of this new constitution is smoke and mirrors of what it really signified: the legalization of Bustamante's carte blanche of permanent control. It is outlined in plain sight that he is made “president for life”, no longer the mere premier of Jamaica, but declared the “national founder” of Jamaica. His protégé and second-in-command, Donald Sangster, would replace him as prime minister. No one expected Sangster to have real power when Bustamante was the one to retain a significant amount of it. Not even Sangster expected it.

A cacophony of camera flashes welcomed the ambassador as he arrived at the Jamaica House with his motorcade. Making his way to the august tables, he noticed Sangster and the JLP delegation from his vantage point. Stiff shoulders and mostly silent, with a few rictus smiles. It simply does not matter to the ambassador if they get strung along unwillingly, as he sat down on his designated seat. As Bustamante made his opening speech, he declared, rather emphatically, that since America foiled “their” plan of having him deposed, he welcomed the Iberians to further assist in Jamaica's development.
strings.JAM_flavor.4.a: The ambassador could not help but make a curt smile.
strings.JAM_flavor.5.desc:
Normally, a trip from Jamaica to Puerto Rico was quick and easy, but today, Edward Seaga had to travel incognito. If anyone knew where he was going or who he was meeting, the chances of him reaching fifty would drop significantly.

After he had reached San Juan, Seaga took a circuitous route to his meet location and surreptitiously left a mark on the side of a building to signal he was ready. Five minutes later, a car showed up to take Seaga to the FBI station house. After being searched, Seaga was brought in to meet with Theodore Shackley, station chief.

“Apologies for the roundabout methods, Mr. Seaga, but you can never be too careful.”

Seaga brushed off the concerns. “No need, it's purely rational. That's a tune I'm willing to hear. These days, all I'm left with is Busta's insanity.” Seaga coughed to clear his throat before continuing. “The man seems to change his mind at the drop of a hat, then change it again when he picks it back up. Dumping an alliance with America for what? The Iberians? The man is half-senile, for God's sake.”

Shackley countered. “Still, he does have a lot of enduring public support.”

“Not among the JLP. The core of the party still exists and is just waiting to pull the rug out from under him. Sangster is Bustamante's pet Prime Minister, but few respect him; I'm not sure he has an independent thought of his own. If we can count on the US's support, we can ensure that Jamaica can come back into the fold, away from Iberia. Otherwise, Jamaica will become poorer, and the United States's position in the Caribbean will diminish. I don't think, Mr. Shackley, that this is in either of our interests.”
strings.JAM_flavor.5.a: You are correct, Mr. Seaga, it certainly isn't.
strings.JAM_flavor_5_tt:
Our position in Jamaica may have been weakened, but we're not out yet.
We'll collaborate with Edward Seaga to get rid of Bustamante.
strings.JAM_flavor.7.desc:
The fanfare outside the King's House did little to mask the unease. Beneath the sun-bleached bunting, the crowd of civil servants and businessmen knew that today was not in fact a celebration, but an elaborate sale. Inside, Sir Alexander Bustamante scrawled his name across the last page of the Iberian Trade Accords. The signature was bold and confident, but the pen trembled slightly as he passed it back to the waiting Iberian envoy, before he shook hands with the ambassador from Madrid and grinned into the blinding light of the cameras.

On paper the deal was fairly straightforward. Iberian corporations would purchase controlling stakes in Jamaica's cobalt mines and refining facilities. In return, the island would receive a lifeline: foreign currency, industrial machinery, and an assurance of “mutual economic development”. Euphemisms aside, the deal was technically far more beneficial to the Jamaicans than the Iberians, who knew perfectly well that cobalt was by no means the island's greatest mineral export, and the mines themselves were unprofitable waste heaps.

The reality behind the deal was that years of crackdowns on dissent had driven the island's investors abroad; the treasury was hollow, and the army was tired of waiting for their pay. The cobalt mines were simply collateral for Jamaica to let in an old colonial master under somewhat better terms than the previous arrangement. As far as Madrid was concerned, they now had an outpost in the Caribbean after only about a century's gap, and the means to begin forcing their way into its economy.

For the workers lying in their shacks and shanties around the mines, the news came as an echo down the shafts. Another foreign name painted on the equipment, another flag stitched on the helmets. 

Bustamante stood on the veranda as the Iberian delegation's motorcade rolled away, a faint breeze tugging at his coat. The bay glittered below, blue and endless. Somewhere in the back of his mind, he wondered if he had only begun a pattern of selling the island away, piece by piece, to those uninterested in her welfare.
Then he pushed those thoughts away and downed a gin and tonic.
strings.JAM_flavor.7.a: And then he had another one.
strings.JAM_flavor.8.desc:
Kingston Harbour was quiet except for the sound of the tide hitting the hulls. A single bulb flickered above the customs shed and irritated Donnie Clarke. There was barely any electricity in the Gardens, but apparently they could spare some for this shithole. They stood around a nondescript crate, stamped with Spanish markings that no one could read. Not that that mattered, since they could hear the rattle of empty magazines inside.

A black car pulled up. Two men stepped out, one of them wearing a pressed shirt despite the heat, the other a six-foot brick of pure muscle. The man in the pressed shirt didn't greet anyone, and only opened his briefcase and handed Clarke an envelope.

“That's for this month,” he said. “The rest moves on the next freighter. The police will be far away the pier for forty-eight hours.”

Clarke counted the notes without looking up. “Last month you said the same,” he said. “Then Customs raided two of my boys' boats.”

Pressed-Shirt didn't argue. He placed another smaller envelope on top of the first. “Consider that an apology.”

Clarke smiled, thin and humourless. “I don't really care who runs the show,” he said. “Just don't make promises you can't keep. My people hear that name, González-Mata - they start thinking someone else owns this place. Some little fop from Spain or Portugal.”

“Someone does,” said the man in the shirt, then nodded toward the crate. “Get it loaded. The ship leaves before dawn.”

Clarke's posse moved quickly. Within minutes, the crate disappeared into a truck and the shed emptied. The two men lingered for a moment, watching from the car through a haze of cigar smoke. By the time they drove off, the only sound left was the water against the pier and the distant echo of drunken laughter from the gangs unloading another shipment. The trade would never stop now. Not at night.
strings.JAM_flavor.9.desc:
Though the Prime Minister's office was playing host to an unusual gathering of people, it remained silent. The Inspector-General of the JCF stood by the window, reading through the latest police reports. Fewer shootings, fewer strikes, fewer headlines. On the surface, things were improving.

Across the table, Luis M. González-Mata flicked ash into a glass tray and waited. “You see?” he said finally. “The numbers speak for themselves.”

The Chief of Defence Staff frowned. “You're paying them to behave. That isn't governance.”

“It's cheaper than a war. And the Prime Minister agrees.”

The door opened. Bustamante entered, moving slower than he used to. “Gentlemen,” he said, taking his seat. “The treasury reports order in Kingston. The docks are working again. People are being fed. That is what matters.”

“At what cost? These gangsters think they're the government now. They collect our payments and call them tribute. We've sold off our - ”

Bustamante cut him off and nodded at an advisor. “We can fight them,” the advisor said, “but we'll bleed the island dry. I've completed a preliminary report here, if you want to consult it. But my conclusion is, simply: they want money, not power. Let's give them what they understand.”

The Prime Minister closed his eyes for a moment, then spoke quietly. “If the people can sleep, we'll call it peace.”

Later that night, an envelope left the Ministry of Finance under police escort. It would reach a warehouse in Tivoli Gardens by morning, one of dozens delivered that week. The men who received it didn't wear uniforms, but they kept their streets quiet.

On the radio, the government announced a “period of stability.” In the alleys, the gangs called it tribute season, and greedily licked their lips. But for now, Jamaica slept.
strings.JAM_flavor.9.a: A fitful sleep is still sleep.
strings.JAM_flavor.10.t: When All You Have is a Banana
strings.JAM_flavor.10.desc:
It was half-past three when Edward Seaga walked into the San Juan station, a smile on his face visible despite his drawn hood. He had grown to enjoy these meetings, despite the hassle of traveling incognito. Though now, Bustamante had more things to worry about than what Edward Seaga was up to.

The preparation for Operation Banana Split had been a complete success. The FBI had successfully cultivated multiple sources in Bustamante's government. Whenever an unflattering report was written, it would be less than a day before it would be exposed by a journalist's “anonymous source.” Busta's labor union was similarly penetrated, and discussions abounded about the lack of faith that the workers had in the President's willingness to defend labor rights, particularly when it came to defending native Jamaicans against Iberian businesses willing to exploit them.

Seaga was even able to suborn criminal organizations to work for him. The most notable of which, the Shower Posse, were happy to burn rival ganja fields and enforce a brutal sort of order in the poorer sections of town and among the unsavory elements. Shackley hadn't been too fond of that element of the operation, but the practical part of his mind quieted his objections; criminals were going to exist, better that they be working for you than against you.

“Mr. Seaga. Let's talk about the future of Jamaica...”
strings.JAM_flavor.10.a: Shackley and Seaga. A match made in heaven.
strings.JAM_flavor.13.desc:
The pristine water from the ocean shimmered and gleamed, the sun a perfect orb in its reflection. The boat rocked intensely amidst the swishing and sloshing of the waves, causing some water to splash onto the emigres and into the boat. Apart from the sounds of the natural world and the inevitable cries from children, the boat was completely silent. 172 Rastafarian refugees were here today. Not one of them wanted to be here, for it to have come to this, yet here they were.

Marcus fiddled with a roll of dope in his hand, rubbing his fingers over it in anxiousness. The waves gave the boat a violent shake, jolting the cannabis from his hands. His knee-jerk reflexes gave him grace, as he caught it mid-air, only three feet above the vast abyss of the sea. He cautiously sunk back into his seat, both out of relief and shock. As he went back to fiddling with his joint, he looked across the deck to see the refugees.

One particular man caught Marcus's eye, Bob Marley, sitting in a boat at the very front of this congregation, the tip of the spear. Marcus began to recollect over those quiet times as he listened to his songs over the radio. In those sorrowful days back in Jamaica — when he questioned his faith and felt all was lost — those songs always brought him back to earth. What he'd give for that familiar feeling right now.

Another thing then catched his eye, just in front of all of the boats the sight of the Florida coastline finally came into view. After a trip that felt like days, if not weeks, despite certainly not being within the time frame of even one day, it's finally coming to an end. That excited relief within Marcus proved contagious, as all the other refugees began to stand in celebration. Then, multiple cars, filled with armed Americans came to the shore, that's when Marcus realized.
strings.JAM_flavor.13.a: Our struggle is only just beginning.
strings.JAM_flavor.16A.desc:
Edward Seaga sat in his office and dialed the 787 number, a military base in San Juan. The heat was unbearable for him, his fan on and windows open as he was waiting for his AC to be fixed. He could hear faint gunshots from outside. Jamaica was teetering on the edge of oblivion. “Hello? Colonel Hart? It's Mr. Seaga,” he said into the phone.

He heard a throat clearing before the colonel responded, “Mr. Seaga, how are you? We're surprised to be hearing from you-” Edward cut in, “Because of the black out? The government buildings have emergency generators and the like.” He looked out the window and saw a sea of black. The lights from Kingston's buildings were gone, now replaced with barrels on fire and screams in the dark.

“Anyways, I've called to tell you that the rumors about Donald Sangster are true. He's died of a stroke a few hours ago. Bustamante can't be contacted by anyone either. No one wants to lead Jamaica it seems.”

“He-he's dead? Oh shit, I've got to put you on hold for a second-” The colonel was cut off by Seaga.
strings.JAM_flavor.16A.a: “Don't worry, I'll be taking the reins back soon.”
strings.JAM_flavor.16B.desc:
Luis González-Mata hurried through Kingston, trying to keep low. Upon piles of rubble men shot and stabbed each other, lit only by fire from barrels. People ran out into the streets to break open fire hydrants, getting relief from the summer's harsh heat. It seemed as if the whole of Jamaica broke when Donald Sangster died.

Bustamante was himself gone, maybe dead, maybe hiding. When the black outs happened he disappeared. Luis was going to Hugh Shearer. If there was anyone who could bring back some stability it would be him, or at least Luis hoped he could.

Luis thought himself better than the average person, scuttling through the darkness terrified, staying holed up in their apartments. He was a smart man, one who lived a life of daring adventures in other countries. Now he was no better than the people of Jamaica he thought were fools, with all their hopes pooled in one man.
strings.JAM_flavor_16_tt: The results of our efforts in Jamaica will be revealed soon.
strings.JAM_flavor.18.desc:
CONFIDENTIAL
TO THE MINISTER OF FOREIGN AFFAIRS

JAMAICA - UNSTABLE SOCIETY

In a recorded telephone call between the Iberian ambassador to Jamaica and Hugh Shearer, Shearer pledged to honor and resume the covert arrangements between the Jamaican government and the Jamaican gangs to keep crime rates low, with remuneration provided to the groups. Despite this, the national yearly rates of extortion, larceny, and murder have reached their highest levels in a decade, with the proliferation of “gang wars” by the dons in support of or against the JLP.

The destruction caused by both the blackout and the hurricane resulted in a big boon for the posses; victims who suffered personally and economically were recruited in droves to gangs rivaling posses in exchange for high payment. This encumbering situation is exacerbated by JLP and PNP party members, including Edward Seaga, a JLP celebrity and former housing minister, who used his connections in Tivoli Gardens to allow loyal posses to expand their territories violently.

Hugh Shearer's cabinet relocated some of the posses' funding to the reconstruction of social services and wrecked infrastructure, stalling the scheme's efficacy. Current economic forecasts foresee little to no growth in Jamaica's economy due to a lack of investors and a dwindling tourism industry.

For the time being, we cannot recommend any actions to reverse this course.
strings.JAM_flavor.18.a: You can't nurture a nation with lies forever.
strings.JAM_flavor.19.desc:
The diplomats in the Half Moon resort were having a period of rest after a lackluster meeting with Shearer's ministers. The Sugar Mill Restaurant was a decent choice for the diplomats to have an impromptu meeting, due to the lack of paying customers.

“You know that the old man can barely speak with that illness wearing him down? I'd be surprised if he'll make it to the end of the year, with the drastic weight loss over the months.” Luis M. González-Mata was busy trying to light a cigar while gossiping with the others.

“And we know Shearer doesn't have the buoyancy nor seniority to handle this untenable mess.” The gentleman speaking donned a navy blazer as he blew his own smoke. “Though that promise of reforming the authoritarian state and releasing some political prisoners may woo some liberals, it does not mean he has it under control with other nefarious groups.”

“The communists?” A bespectacled diplomat questions him.

“Fucking donkey, the massives!” Luis's sudden outburst made the garçon whip his head towards the table from afar. “The feeble fool I once trusted can't handle the deal properly, so now they are running amok again in the streets.” Luiz pours scorn in a hushed tone, brooding to his audience.

“So that's it?” The bald diplomat in a tan suit quietly exclaimed. “We just let Bustamante get pushed into the shadows while we let his successor, the highfalutin baboso, try to keep America at bay by stopping them from pushing cocaine?”

No words were exchanged for the rest of the meeting. At the end, the garçon simply glanced at them when they left the premises.
strings.JAM_flavor.19.a: They're just going to watch the ships pass by.

FROM AGENT DUNNE
MEMORANDUM FOR THE PRESIDENT

SUBJECT: INTEL REPORT ON JAMAICA

1. Hugh Shearer, assuming the role of Prime Minister of Jamaica following Donald Sangster's passing during the blackout wave, had relaxed the country's censorship laws and promised further social and economic reforms after taking office. However, he will not respond to demands to amend Sir Alexander Bustamante's titles as president for life and national founder, maintaining Bustamante's legacy as a “liberator” and “champion of Jamaicans”.

2. Leaked sources point out that Shearer had not changed the tenuous relationship with the criminal gangs responsible for the increased drug and weapon smuggling into the United States. He still maintains the agreement to provide capital to the gangs in exchange for social stability. Intelligence also investigated Bustamante's dwindling public appearances and discovered he suffers from a “long illness”. It is predicted that he now wields less executive control over Shearer as his health further deteriorates. Our political ally in the JLP, Edward Seaga, now holds less influence in the party since Shearer's ascension and is unable to impact Shearer's rule. Seaga's reduced role will affect any future operations in Jamaica.

3. Despite continued financing and support from the Iberian Union, high-level corruption is the main issue surrounding Kingston, which showcases that criminal gangs now hold considerable sway over the nation. Jamaica's internal situation continues to show no signs of improvement, and its future remains unpredictable.
strings.JAM_flavor.21.desc:
A turbulent journey from rubbing shoulders with syndicates of Tivoli Gardens to finally molding the country himself, with Shackley utilising the political chaos, beginning with the hurricane darkening the entire island, as the corollary. Seaga now sat across from the ambassador and diplomats, pinned with the American flag next to their right lapel.

A diplomat from the other side questioned Bustamante's absence during the meeting. “That old man is too old to hold a pen for a minute longer.” A few chuckles can be heard from both aisles, from Seaga's dry quip.

“The Treaty of Kingston is a stepping stone to restoring our nations' amicable relations, and a stronger economic partnership between the U.S and Jamaica is requisite for enough opportunities to bring derelict neighbourhoods on the mend.” Seaga stood in front of the podium beside the American ambassador, shortly after signing the new treaty, reciting an inconspicuous Aesopian speech with a robotic tone for the cameras.

The blackout allowed the posses to wreak havoc in the streets once again, especially with the newfound instability of Sangster's unfortunate passing. With increased crime rates and the interminable smuggling of cocaine and marijuana northwards, Seaga used his connections with Tivoli Gardens to handle it, in exchange for opportunities to overpower rival gangs' unreconstructed loyalty to the PNP and Iberia. For Jamaica and the Don of the Shadow Posse, it was a win-win deal.

“Mr. Prime Minister, with investors still wary regarding reported shootouts and kidnappings in neighbourhoods all over Jamaica, how can you respond to this concern?” The ABC logo on the microphone identified who the reporter was when he hid behind the camera flashes as he posed his unbidden query. Seaga's practiced cadence in his response masked his great displeasure.
strings.JAM_flavor.21.a: “Firstly, these criminals will be dealt with in time...”
strings.JAM_flavor.22.desc:
The sunlight from the clear blue sky felt overbearing on Luis González-Mata's head. Six years of work guiding Bustamante in Iberia's orbit had gone to waste, as the men from the JCF accompanied him to his flight back home.

Sangster's death and Bustamante's disappearance practically plunged Jamaica into chaos. He witnessed Seaga make the derisive chess move to overthrow the lackey and consolidate control in the JLP. By then, the writing on the wall spells out that Mata will be the first snakebit target. With the old man out of reach during the bout of anarchy, his hands were tied, and fate rewarded him by being declared “persona non grata”.

He carried a resigned expression as the men in blue marched him from the tarmac towards the passenger door. Seaga had outed him as a spy who bribed gangs responsible for the deaths of hundreds and millions in damages in the midst of the blackout. To implicate Mata as the scapegoat? For the same crime, the great Augean stable of the JLP took part in? He found it quite sardonic.

What now? Being ousted by a former ally of your nation is a black mark on anyone's portfolio, so he expected an early retirement from SECED once he returned to Madrid. Busta will rot away in house arrest while he keeps his nominal titles, so history might show that in the end, he was all hat and no cattle. Mata won't miss working with a fool like him.

A pensive smile crept in as he peered through his window at his seat. He will miss this side of the Atlantic Ocean.
strings.JAM_flavor.25.desc:
“Why did I drag myself to this fucking island? Augustin had been asking himself this question for the entire past week. Right now, he was shaking inside an armored bus that was slowly ramming through an endless human crowd with a strained roar. Rocks, pieces of rebar, and other trash drummed like hail against the plating. Next to him, gripping their assault rifles with white-knuckled fingers, sat two armed guards - raw recruits, younger than himself. A sea raged outside the windows: thousands of fired miners and their embittered, starving families had blockaded the streets of Kingston. The police were nowhere to be seen - along with the economic collapse, a complete collapse of the Jamaican state had arrived.

Why is there no news from out there? Augustin had received his last letter from home exactly two weeks ago, and then all communications were cut. Back in the motherland, communists, Falangists, republicans, monarchists - it seemed the entire political spectrum had mixed in the primordial soup of the Iberian Wars. When Madrid and Lisbon went up in flames, the state corporations cut off the oxygen. One hundred and seventy-five. One hundred and seventy-five mines on the island ground to a halt overnight, spitting tens of thousands of destitute workers onto the streets.

Why do they look at us like that? To the Black Jamaicans, the few Iberians who still remained on the island had overnight become traitors and the embodiment of pure evil, because they, unlike the locals, somehow still had jobs. The malice-contorted faces beyond the bulletproof glass didn't know the most important thing: these jobs would last a month at most. Investors were panic-dumping their assets, and the last corporation was also about to flee the sinking island. To the muffled thuds of rocks striking the bus, Augustin could only pray that the company, while evacuating its capital, wouldn't leave him behind on this cursed island.”
strings.JAM_flavor.26.desc:
FBI Intelligence Report: Bustamante's Plea

Following the collapse of the Iberian Union and the peninsula's subsequent economic breakdown, Jamaica's central bank has entered a state of bankruptcy. The suspension of many national programs and other government-funded projects due to a withdrawal of Iberian corporate investments precedes a surge in unemployment, and in other cases, criminality. Alexander Bustamante's Jamaican Labour Party cabinet is seeking an American bailout, without other options.

Bustamante has, therefore, requested a meeting with American ambassadors in order to convey the current crisis in Jamaica as a humanitarian concern, citing the nation's reliance on foreign funding, and its current lack thereof, to be in the interest of the United States for mending its relations with the island nation. He offers to provide the same concession as was provided to enterprises of the Iberian Union if the United States government guarantees renewed support to the JLP-led government. However, he refused any suggestion of regime change or internal reforms.

On account of the JLP's current domestic unpopularity and Bustamante's unwillingness to accept American counsel, Jamaica will likely face significant political instability and undergo a depression, provided Bustamante remains in his position as head of state. The country is predicted to be at a high risk of social collapse in the short term.
strings.JAM_flavor.26.a: Stubborn as always, not a bit of humility in his mouth.
strings.JAM_flavor_26_tt:
Due to the collapse of the Iberian Union, Bustamante has come crawling back to us!
...But we have not forgotten about his defiance, and a traitor is always owed his due.
strings.JAM_flavor.27.desc:
“We, for one, are impressed with Billy Strachan. Few men have shown such a firm capacity to resist fascism, and few men have shown such a strong commitment to the ideals of decolonization and pan-Africanism as Strachan. Washington will find itself far more challenged than it may expect...” - The Black Panther, Editorial, {date}...

“...and I completely condemn Billy Strachan's coup in Jamaica. Bolshevism has failed Russia, failed China, and is now due to fail Jamaica. When radicals like the Black Panther Movement claim to want equality, all they want is equality in tying your noose. The Bolshevist strand of equality will not be satisfied with one island...” - Remarks from Richard Russell Jr., 14:00 {date}...

“The United States was stuck. The natural impulse was to issue a condemnation, but anything further and public would stretch American diplomatic efforts. Cuba and Mexico were both already distant enough from the American sphere, and Castro made particular note to commend the Jamaican revolutionaries. As such, American efforts against Strachan drifted towards espionage.” - Potemkin in Portmore: The United States and the Caribbean Left, 1959-72...

“The Act Condemning Jamaican Extremism, which will implement sanctions on a number of Jamaican products and will issue an explicit condemnation of its new government, passed through the House of Representatives by a margin of 432-0, and is expected to pass through the Senate today unanimously. However, civil rights organizations have lambasted it as an unconscionable violation of Jamaican sovereignty...” - ABC Television Broadcast, {date}, 15:00
strings.JAM_flavor.27.a: A revolution abroad, a convulsion within.
strings.JAM_flavor.28.t: By the Skin of His Teeth
strings.JAM_flavor.28.desc:
Leaning down slightly, Luis González-Mata struggled to hide himself from the cameras held by journalists, their chorus failing to pierce the wall of the Iberian security forces fleeing around him. Above them, the blades of a helicopter whirred impatiently, drowning out the questions being fielded at them. As he entered the vehicle, he slinked out of view, hiding behind the door, unable to justify sitting down to himself. Not that the journalists would stay much longer, he thought. As soon as the Bolshevists had their way, they'd be out. Or else.

That a Jamaican Revolution had even occurred was his first mistake. He had followed the growing radicalization of the Jamaican populace for months, but had never expected it to be nearly this advanced, or to proceed so rapidly. By the time street protests had devolved into revolution, he was only just getting in touch with what members of his spy network hadn't already been killed. Bustamante was to blame for that. He was never a secure ally, thought González-Mata, and always liked to pretend he had more control than he actually did.

Of course, his immediate priority was escaping. His helicopter was chartered to land a few kilometers out from Managua, but the journey back could not be chartered in time. He had an identity planned, of course; for the next day, he would be Miguel Ortega-Iglesias, a businessman and owner of a car factory in Valladolid, visiting Managua to discuss the idea of using natural rubber, and now looking to return through Madrid. But what was to come of him once he was back?

Iberia had lost a major ally in the Caribbean, with no warning, and a lot of good agents alongside them. He knew they'd want a scapegoat of some kind, and that he was perfect for a cull. He didn't know whether to expect a demotion to another branch of Iberia's spy network in America, or to expect his imminent removal. As the helicopter took off, he finally crumpled down, head planted firmly in his hands.
strings.JAM_flavor.28.a: And as the revolution claimed the mind of one more individual.
strings.JAM_flavor.29.desc:
On the streets of Queens, there was the smell of grilled meat and the sight of green and black triangles flanked by golden stripes flooding the air. The Jamaican emigre community had taken the foundation of the new republic with impromptu block parties, excited at the success of the revolution. As the food and beer passed from hand to hand, there was one man, smiling and joking with the revelers, who was not smiling.

Lincoln Bullock's family had emigrated from Jamaica when he was a boy, and he had made a name for himself as both a bright kid and a popular one. He had been recruited by the FBI right out of school, not that he needed much convincing after his father had been shot by two Nazi sympathizers during an anti-fascist rally. He was bilingual, easy-going, and above all, a patriot. A natural fit to work, in his own small way, for the Caribbean office.

After the revolution, there had been fear that the PNP, always close with the emigre communities in the US, would feel emboldened and create domestic unrest for the United States. If they had joined hands with the black nationalist movements, they might pose a problem. Some dreaming fools might believe a revolution could succeed anywhere, but what Lincoln feared was the smaller things - violent protest that left another little boy without a father.

“Isn't it crazy what's going on on the island? Finally got a place that's ours, nobody else's. I'm thinking of going back, once I save up. Best I see it for myself.”

“Not a bad idea,” Lincoln lied, “though I think I'll wait a bit for things to calm down first. You never know, you know?”
strings.JAM_flavor.29.a: Lincoln smiled, he joked, but above all, he listened.
strings.JAM_flavor.31.desc:
In the smoky halls of San Juan Station, Theodore Shackley read the report in his hands. Operation Rotten Cardinal had finally finished moving money to keep the JLP propped up. Manley had hoped to decimate the JLP with the riots and secure an uncontested political future for himself. An easy enough idea, but Manley should have learned from the success of his own movement: killing an idea was hard work.

Money didn't talk, but it did make words easier to hear. Labor unions listened when Manley discussed working conditions, but when an FBI operative pointed out that Manley would pressure the union to ensure that his people were put in leadership roles, that had made them receptive to propping up the JLP to hedge their bets, with a little cash in their pockets, of course. Organized crime was a fact of life in Jamaica, and when the FBI pointed out that Manley would use them as a scapegoat to score political points for himself, they became a bit more receptive to their talking points and their bribes. Other politicians were the easiest of all; Manley made no secret about his ambitions. Any politician with ambition of his own would know that there couldn't be two suns in the sky, but anyone who even wanted to genuinely serve his country would know that losing favor could mean the end of everything, and that meant insurance through the JLP was a safe bet.

A tailored homily for every group, and now all they needed was a figurehead to rally behind. After Bustamante's spectacular fall, a new figure needed to arise from the ashes, and this time, it had to be someone much more reliable. A figure perhaps, that already had ties to the San Juan office and so could benefit from analysis from back home, and that could reliably ensure that the flock would be sufficiently motivated to work for the greater good of all.
strings.JAM_flavor.31.a: “Edward Seaga. He's who we want for this.” Shackley extinguished his cigarette and put the file down.
strings.JAM_flavor.33.desc:
A dream years in the making was coming to an end. Peter sighed as he hung up the phone, closing yet another business account and getting the money out of the country. He tried to ignore the sounds of the construction crews taking the kitchen out the back, piece by piece. He could have left it behind, but it was worth enough on the resale that it was worth getting out of Jamaica before the hammer came down.

All Peter wanted was to own a hotel, to bring people joy on their vacations and make a living in the process. And for a while, life had been good. Profits were up and he was hoping to expand, but then came Manley and the revolution. Instability was bad in the short term, but when Manley took over and started his rhetoric, Peter knew his days were numbered. The banks would be broken into, and all foreign-held assets would be seized, and anything Manley wanted, especially if it was owned by an American, would be taken without compensation. So all his hard work, up in smoke because one man's greed could never be sated.

Over the radio, the announcer gave the news that the tungsten mines on the island were to be nationalized. They played back Manley's quote, where he spoke of tungsten's national importance and his promise to improve working conditions in the mines. Then he stated, “We seek a democratic path to socialism, we seek equality and dignity for all. We are not tyrants here to say that we shall take everything. All we want is for our workers to be treated like people, for them to own and achieve their own fulfillment just like any other man would.” Just words, thought Peter. Since a foreigner and a businessman didn't count as a person, then he was most certainly exempt from Manley's high-minded protestations. He didn't want to hurt Jamaica, but they seemed intent on harming him.
strings.JAM_flavor.33.a: Peter could hear Manley's voice over the radio quiver. The bastard didn't even have the decency to lie well.
strings.JAM_flavor.36.desc:
America continues to play a light hand against communists from the West Indies

Adam McCray, Cultural Correspondent, National Review

No matter what this government claims, it is clear that {usa_getleader} doesn't truly care about combatting extremism. Nothing about this is clearer than them allowing for Bob Marley to play songs over here. In the West Indies, Bob Marley has already become a household name, as has his band. Playing a new genre of music called “reggae,” a style of music notable for having a far slower tempo, and for its heavy reliance on drums and bass guitars for its melody.

Bob Marley first became active in 1963, and has published a number of albums with his band, The Wailers, but it was his own work that played over the bar in Harlem today, with his singles reaching record numbers. In 1966, he converted from Catholicism to Rastafarianism, a fringe cult that believes the former King of Ethiopia is the second coming, and that God exists in everyone.

Any biography has to consider his fringe views. A devout communist, he is a vocal supporter of groups such as the African National Congress and has staunchly condemned South Africa's struggle against their extremism. He has also attacked the United States as being “as imperialist as Germany and Japan,” and also openly smokes pot for “meditation.”

Men such as this are adored by hippies and pot-smokers nationally, and he has become a figurehead for these bums, but he does admittedly have some musical talent. If you still want to listen to this new wave riling up hippies across the nation, Bob Marley will be playing again at Harlem on Tuesday, and will play in bars in Chicago, Boston, Los Angeles, and Montreal over the next two weeks.
strings.JAM_flavor.36.a: Just take care to step over any vagrants high on his work.
strings.JAM_flavor.38.desc:
Compared to the streets of Kingston, the American embassy was remarkably refined. A shame, Michael Manley thought, that such development didn't extend much further. He knew that talks with the American ambassador on debt relief and on economic aid would come with implicit demands, but hoped that he could at least swing them into patience. He received no such welcome.

“We have a lot of money, Michael,” replied the ambassador, interrupting an outreached hand, “but we won't just plug the holes of an economic basketcase.”

Michael Manley knew what was going to come, but pushed aside his concerns. “Give us a few years, and I know we'll exceed your expectations.”

“I hope your optimism is well placed.” The ambassador threw up a V sign. “We won't negotiate on either of these. We want full democratization, and we expect you to change track on your hostility to American business.”
Halting for a second, Michael Manley tried to work the issue. “I arrested those responsible for the worst excesses, and I guarantee that nex-”

“I'm not stupid, Mike.” Raising a finger, he muted the discussion. “You can flatter me all you like, but American businesses have been rankling at the way you've been nationalizing your country's economy.” With a flick of his hand, he drew out a cigar. “Reverse your recent nationalizations, or else you'll have to command your plantations penniless.”

Michael Manley shook his head as he considered a path forward. Surrendering Jamaica's sovereignty over its economy was disastrous, but the ambassador had a point. Jamaica needed the aid too desperately. And so, squirming in his chair painted red, he surrendered his time to preserve ambition.
strings.JAM_flavor.38.a: The King issues a proclamation from his Castle.
strings.JAM_flavor.50.desc:
Edward Seaga was recognized when he traveled, so when he needed to meet with people that Manley didn't want him to meet, it meant a little razzle-dazzle. He'd send one of his bodyguards out in a hat and his coat to buy something inconspicuous - a six-pack of beer or some junk food, anything that a man who worked as hard as he did would need to take the edge off at 11 at night. Then he'd wear a wig and pad his coat and drive off, as if he were one of his staff taking off for the night. A simple shake of his tail, then he could meet his benefactors. Manley had been more and more on edge lately as his situation deteriorated. It wouldn't be long before Seaga would need to put more effort into his steps.

“Gentleman, how fares Mister Shackley?” Seaga greeted the three stone-faced FBI agents. Shackley had been arranging more meetings of late, and that had plenty of portents, both for fair and for foul.

“He's well. But we're not here for pleasantries, Mister Seaga. We think it might actually be time to start making arrangements for a more...active role in the changing of the leadership situation.”

If Shackley's assets were this clinical, it meant that something was serious. Shackley was amiable enough, but the mission's importance always meant that his smoother edges were worn down when it came time to get something done. It made him a great station chief, and why he'd never make director of the Bureau.

“Of course. Let's outline our options. Despite everything, Manley retains support among his loyal cadre, so we should keep in mind that even if the entire island hates him, there will be plenty of people willing to dance to his tune. If you like the song, it seems, then you can't help but tap your feet.”
strings.JAM_flavor.50.a: In the night, the FBI laid out the steps, and Seaga wondered if it would be enough to carry the floor.
strings.JAM_flavor.51.desc:
Office of the Central Intelligence Agency, surveillance recording transcript.
Recorded on site in downtown Georgetown, relevant names redacted for posterity.

REDACTED 1: “-re not blind to what's been going on in Kingston.”
SEAGA: (Pointed) “Aren't you now?”
REDACTED 2: “It's the reason we are all here, we can sort you out, sort this out.”
REDACTED 1: “Jamaica is going to get the sweetheart treatment, humanitarian aid camps, development subsidies, trade deals. No big announcements per se, just things coming down the pipe.”
SEAGA: (Pause) “And the violence?”
REDACTED 1: (Longer Pause) “I'm sorry?”
SEAGA: “The violence in Kingston, reports on the crime rate.”
REDACTED 2: “I-I've bits of it on CNN...”
SEAGA: (Hushed) “Look, I am not ungrateful and I speak on behalf of our people-”
REDACTED 2: “Oh, n-no. We understand! Very clearly.”
SEAGA: “I don't need to remind you of everything that's happened lately in the Caribbean. Santa Domingo, Havana...Kingston is not there yet, thank God, but if this gets any worse...”
REDACTED 1: (Pause) “...I see.”
REDACTED 2: “We can only promise so much, we'll see what we can do. Hopefully, it won't come to that.
strings.JAM_flavor.52.desc:
For a few days after the Jamaican Revolution had begun in earnest, the offices of the Jamaican Labour Party had been left in a state of limbo, occupied only by a few members of the Black Star Brigade awaiting orders. Upon new orders, however, this silence was broken. Almost suddenly, each desk drawer was harvested in turn, each paper in each office torn apart for signs of dissent, or of gifts, or of imports, thrown onto piles and sent away in turn. Nails in a coffin.

By the morning, Billy Strachan roared onto the radio with stunning revelations. The Jamaican Labour Party, and especially Alexander Bustamante, had happily tied itself to the Iberian government, allowing Iberia to smuggle goods through its ports in return for a premium on embargoed goods. In reports echoed by excited newsanchors, fascism had lost its anchoring with the revolution. From Jamaica, it could finally be uprooted, expunged and consigned to history.

Throughout the afternoon, Montego Bay Airport swelled from full to bursting. What few Iberian citizens had yet to leave quickly found themselves overwhelmed by members of the Jamaican Labour Party, hoping to stretch their local campaigns to pivotal trades in Lisbon or Madrid or Casablanca, or to stunning subversions of fascism in New York, or Toronto, or to wherever would take them. As the sky turned a burning orange, queues buckled to haggling as confusion mounted. Few would have their questions answered.

As night fell once again, and as Jamaican air traffic was shuttered, the arrests began. At first, it was only the mid-level functionaries, those specifically named by diplomats and spies as helping with their cause in some way. Their testimonies only allowed for such remit to be extended. Over the next day, a full list of Jamaican Labour Party members was drawn up. Most were visited and questioned, and many were arrested, charged with reactionary practice, and sentenced to life in prison.
strings.JAM_flavor.52.a: One side of the Atlantic loses its wire to its other half.

FROM THOMAS COBELn
MEMORANDUM FOR THE PRESIDENT

SUBJECT: STATE OF JAMAICAN POPULAR REPUBLIC AND ITS EXILES

After the recent overthrow of the government, the JPR has been steadily stabilizing its regime. The government is unlikely to collapse on its own unless intervention is used. With the new government in power, JLP members, business elites, and disaffected liberals from the PNP have fled to Miami.

The FBI has been in contact with these exiles, with JLP member Edward Seaga being an important asset for the bureau. Some exiles have made requests and petitions to the government to help them return to Jamaica by helping enact a counterrevolution. Agents have reported a close camaraderie and extreme desire to return among the group.

If aided, the exiles could create unrest and help with subversive activities in Jamaica, perhaps even leading to their requested counterrevolution, or an invasion of the island.
strings.JAM_flavor.54.t: Jamaican Opposition Movements Begin to Organize
strings.JAM_flavor.54.desc:
TOP SECRET/{date}

FROM THEODORE SHACKLEY

MEMORANDUM FOR THE PRESIDENT

SUBJECT: COORDINATION OF ANTI-BOLSHEVIST FORCES IN JAMAICA

1. A group of Jamaican exiles amenable to CIA efforts has landed in Jamaica in recent days and has succeeded in coordinating opposition to the Strachan regime. There is a definite opposition within the island, but a combination of geography, government repression, and personal infighting has greatly limited their capacities.

2. Our communication has been limited, but consistent, and provides a clear picture of Jamaica's opposition. Although reduced, Iberian smuggling networks have survived and are still actively spreading weaponry, though they are vying with numerous homegrown gangs for hegemony. A number of former Jamaican Labour Party supporters have also begun to form small entities, though they have yet to become firmly militant.

3. Existing criminal networks will not be viable governing partners, but their organization and their capacity to reduce government strength make them a potential ally for now. Iberia seems to have abandoned the country entirely, which will provide an easy offramp for the JLP to become far more amenable to American influence.
strings.JAM_flavor.55.desc:
Winston nervously fiddled with the handle of his worn leather briefcase. This entire week had felt like elaborate torture. It began with a humiliating economy-class flight on a standard commercial airliner, and continued with seven days of waiting in a faceless Washington motel. For seven days, he and his colleagues had worked the phones non-stop, fawning over junior senators' clerks and begging for meetings with the very American businessmen whose assets the people's republic had so proudly expropriated.

And now, the heavy oak doors opened. Winston stepped into the office of the US Secretary of State and almost choked. Sitting to the left of the host were them - the leaders of the Jamaican exile community from Miami, flashing smug smirks. No chairs had been provided for the delegation from Kingston.

Looking into the eyes of the American minister, Winston was already visualizing the impending interrogation minute by minute. He knew exactly what was coming. Dry, striking questions about what they wanted, why Washington should believe them, and what concessions they were willing to make. And he would have to, swallowing the remnants of his revolutionary pride, lay it all out: begging for loans, promising sweeping privatization in favor of US corporations, and swearing to return Jamaica to the fold of the OFN. He frantically rehearsed the hardest answer in his mind-for the moment the Secretary would nod at the beaming exiles and demand their return to the government.

Winston exhaled and took a step forward. The doors closed behind the delegation.

And the meeting ended...“

FROM THEODORE SHACKLEY

MEMORANDUM FOR THE PRESIDENT

SUBJECT: SHOOTOUT BETWEEN RED JAMAICAN MILITIAS AND EVACUATING ANGLO-CANADIAN FORCES

1. Canadian efforts to evacuate Canadian and British civilians have met resistance from Jamaica's Black Star Brigade, headed by revolutionary leader Billy Strachan, with a shootout happening at 03:45 last night around Ocho Rios. Casualties did occur, but were limited and didn't seem to have dramatically impacted the course of this operation.

2. RCMP marines have been involved in the evacuations and have adhered to their expected schedule. The shootout occurred largely between individuals, but our communique with Ottawa indicates that this was likely an ambush. Both sides only experienced the loss of individual soldiers, who are now being posthumously valorized, and both have declared victory.

3. Such developments are troubling, but our options are limited. Canadian strategy with this evacuation was reckless, but hasn't led to any civilian harm, and any criticism will likely be met with a harsh backlash from Canada. Our own efforts to evacuate personnel from Jamaica should be hastened, but no other changes should be imminently made.

Cigarette smoke drifted lazily toward the ceiling. Marcus, a functionary of the People's National Party, stared at the Canadian investor sitting across from him. The man was spewing curses and threats, but Marcus merely waited patiently for a pause.

“Listen, Mr. Davis. We are offering to buy out seventy-five percent of the shares in your tungsten mine at, let's say, government rates,” Marcus intertwined his fingers. “The state takes over all management, logistics, and union relations. You do absolutely nothing and simply collect your dividends from the remaining share.”

The Canadian turned purple, calling it legalized robbery. After a tense but predictable negotiation, they settled on fifty-five percent in favor of Kingston. Marcus barely hid a smile: this was the exact figure the party had initially planned due to a banal lack of funds for a full buyout. As a guarantee, a copy of a fresh government decree was slid across the table-Strachan's official order suspending forced nationalization. Weighing the risks, the Canadian realized: it was better to earn passive income and retain the option to sell the rest later than to lose everything right here and now. He gave a curt nod, scribbled his signature, and left the room.

Left alone, Marcus let out a sigh of relief and clicked the knob on the radio. Yes, the denizens of the White House still didn't trust Strachan and considered them radicals, but now few people cared. The economy had avoided collapse, and rumors of an imminent counterrevolution had dissipated. Suddenly, the solemn voice of an announcer came through the speaker: the Revolutionary Committee was officially relinquishing its emergency powers. The country was preparing for the first free elections in the history of the new Jamaica.
strings.JAM_flavor.57.a: Putting the house in order doesn't mean burning it down.
strings.JAM_flavor.60.desc:
This was clearly a mistake.

Oh, of course, she'd already known long before she'd even booked the flight down to Kingston with her meager doctoral stipend. Yes, she was young, much younger than most attendees. A woman, no less, and not a name carrying any of the weight of Archimède or Madame Blouin. Worst of all sins: she was a Yank, hailing from the very imperialist heart those gathered here were plotting the fall.

Yet she'd also done more than her own fair share of organizing. Fellow students had rallied and marched down the streets of San Diego to her call, roaring for the rights of those suffering under the same oppressive yoke. She'd clashed against those of her civil rights comrades who denied a woman's lot deserved just as much to be fought for, as she'd sneered at the others who'd dismissed her peddling of dialectics and class consciousness as a white man's thing.

But witnessing the fire, pure and unbridled, that had just occurred within these four walls had seemingly rendered it all so pointless.

Not just hers, but the whole struggle back home that still dared label itself revolutionary. While all they could ever hope to achieve was to propel a slightly less bigoted suit to the White House and earn some token recognition that'd never shield them from a Klan bonfire, the people assembled here were kindling something so, so much more; so why was she walking down the steps of a lecture hall still half-full of the firebrands of Caribbean socialism, trying to chance a meet with-

“A word, Mr. Strachan?” But as soon as the sentence had left her mouth, so did the doubts from her mind, once more replaced by the same poise and confidence that had already brought her so far. Because if she could bring but a spark of this fire home... “Oh, I apologize. Where are my manners?”
strings.JAM_flavor.60.a: “Angela Davis,” she continued, raising her hand for a shake. “CPUSA.”

BY JOHN LINQUIST

MIAMI, {date} — Bob Marley, founding member and leader of the Wailers, arrived at Miami International at around 3 p.m. from Strachan International to commence his tour to promote his upcoming album, Soul Rebels. However, TSA agents stationed there had denied passage for the musician on grounds of “geopolitical concerns”. The Wailers thereafter announced the cancellation of the tour appearances soon after returning to Kingston.

A spokesman on behalf of the Transportation Security Administration, in response to outcry from fans of the reggae artist, stated the dangerous affiliations with the Strachan regime as the main factor for denied entrance.

“To ensure the stability of our nation's political atmosphere, it is prudent to not allow any alleged unespied persons-of-interest to inoculate any radical ways of thought into the American people.” — an excerpt from the published statement.

Civil rights organizations had decried the decision to disallow the tour and impute the Wailers as unjust. Whitney Young, executive director of the National Urban League, a flagship organization aimed at promoting civic equality, expressed his dissatisfaction through a phone interview. Mr. Young described the move as a “hindrance to Black empowerment” and expressed that the cancellations of the tour may enervate the public's attention to racial equality.

Since the violent revolution had overthrown Bustamante from power, the nascent left-wing regime in Jamaica had a continuously contentious bilateral relationship with the United States...

“...I'll give it to the Jamaicans, even teetering on the edge of economic ruin, the eggshell is still holding. They're completely isolated, they have both an energy and a fuel crisis, and yet, the people won't simply just get rid of Strachan.”

“Well, killing your opposition will do that. True believers will starve rather than admit failure.”

“Despite the fact that they can barely function domestically, they still manage to cause instability when they can. Whether it's fellow reds in the Caribbean or expatriates in the United States, they can certainly cause a lot of problems for all of us. We'd better nip this in the bud before someone else does it for us.”

“Well, there's always the direct approach. A full naval invasion of the island due to Strachan's actions is a possibility. Jamaica doesn't have the manpower to resist a Marine landing.”

“That would kill our reputation on the world stage. If we're worried about domestic discontent stirred up from Jamaica, imagine what it could do when the Japanese and the Mexicans would have inroads into the very same communities...with deeper pockets.”

“Edward Seaga has bands of exiles willing to fight for him. If we could provide naval and air support for a landing, we could allow them to fight, then assist them in establishing a pliable government. He already has most of the expertise needed in his cadre. A higher risk of failure, of course, but much less pushback - it looks like a Jamaican internal dispute. Everyone knows it isn't, but appearance counts for a lot.”
