From: Office of South American Affairs
Memorandum for the Director
Subject: Jamaican Trends and Future Operations

The self-proclaimed Jamaican Popular Republic has moderated its previous radical communist attitudes in the recent past. However, the leadership remains committed to hardline beliefs, and it is believed that the moderate direction is a concession to practicality and avoids foreign and domestic blowback. Prime Minister Richard Hart is believed to hold sincere belief in communism and is unlikely to abandon nationalization efforts or utilizing anti-American rhetoric to buttress domestic support and distract the population from concerns of food scarcity and political repression. Jamaica, under Richard Hart, remains a threat to American-owned property in the Caribbean, and a base of operation for future subversive activity and potential foreign intelligence in the region.

However, Hart's political party, the People's Freedom Movement, requires coalition support from the moderate People's National Party under their leader, Michael Manley. The FBI has proposed to provide political support to Manley's PNP in the hopes of fracturing the PNP-PFM coalition, increasing political gridlock and eroding confidence in the PFM and Hart's political leadership. If the PNP can become a more effective and capable political faction, then Hart and the PFM can become discredited in the eyes of the Jamaican people, and they can be returned to a more pro-American alignment.

The proposal involves simple electioneering support, bankrolling political materials, and helping underwrite the cost of electoral staff and campaign workers. The risk of exposure is minimal, and most options operate well within Jamaican domestic law.
strings.JAM_flavor.69.desc:
“The PFM have promised us prosperity, and look what they've given us. Hart speaks of the struggle of the workers, but grows rich while we suffer. Half of us fear for our jobs, the other half have nothing to eat but his empty words! Where is the workers' paradise he promised? His red fire has burned us, and the People's National Party is the only path to prosperity and pride!” The stump speech had been making the rounds across the country, attacking the PFM and Hart in particular. In different neighborhoods, the speech was tweaked and crafted to fit the audience, but the thesis was always the same. Hart had ruined Jamaica with his extreme beliefs, and the PNP would do better by breaking off from the coalition and running the country themselves. To any outside observer, it was the natural backlash to Hart's economic failure. Few things could galvanize a people like shared hardship.

One thing that could was the electioneering support of the American government. Smartly-printed pamphlets and posters filled every PNP office. Talking points and demographic research found their way into the hands of speechwriters and campaign managers. Letters from Jamaican emigres abroad found their way to family members still on the island, urging them to switch their vote and save their home. The fire in the PNP was very real, but it was stoked and fed carefully by hands from Washington DC.

The largest cracks began to form when Edward Seaga endorsed former members of the Jamaican Labour Party to join the PNP. This groundswell of support gave the PNP the chance to contest the PFM on their own terms. If the PNP left the coalition, it could trigger new elections that the PFM had a very real shot of losing. Hart had projected a strong front, but while the exterior was hardened by fire, the core seemed almost ready to snap under the heat.

FROM THEODORE SHACKLEY

MEMORANDUM FOR THE PRESIDENT

SUBJECT: VICTORY OF JAMAICAN RADICALS IN ELECTION

1. Our previous efforts to platform moderates within the Jamaican Popular Republic were in vain. The People's Freedom Movement has won with a resounding victory and will ensure that Richard Hart remains Prime Minister. Moderate elements have been largely secluded and will only come to power via regime change.

2. The elections were conducted with relatively little state interference, but those classed as dissidents were totally barred from participating, and only Michael Manley provided a meaningful alternative. Richard Hart declared victory early, but his initial confidence was well-founded. Further collectivization and nationalization efforts are due, and Hart has explicitly condemned American efforts.

3. At this stage, the only means of gaining a sympathetic ally in Jamaica will be through a coup. Opposition to Hart's rule is disorganized, but present, and should be given far greater funding. Michael Manley is unwilling to engage in a coup, but deputies in the People's National Party, as well as exiled opposition figures like Edward Seaga, could be viable successors.
strings.JAM_flavor.79.desc:
CONFIDENTIAL
TO THE MINISTER OF FOREIGN AFFAIRS

Jamaica - Caribbean

The recent collapse of oil prices and the resulting economic crisis it has brought has now been extended to the Caribbean. Recent reports from Kingston indicate that Jamaica has been hit particularly hard by these developments. Bustamante has begun placing pressure on Iberian diplomats in the area, pushing for us to bailout Jamaica and to issue debt forgiveness, in return offering some significant concessions on access to plantations should we accede.

Although he has privately presented this as part of relief efforts, the root cause is barely related. Reckless spending means he now risks losing control over the gangs he pays off, and without this relief, they will become far more assertive, threatening his central authority. Without a bailout, we also risk Bustamante turning towards the United States or towards Mexico, likely highlighting the risks of a refugee crisis. Both countries have access to significant oil reserves, as do Guyana and Venezuela, and would be happy to reclaim influence in the area. We would be the inevitable losers in this exchange, as would our companies in the area.

Whether we have the funds to afford such a bailout is questionable, but whether we can afford to lose them is also questionable. It will be difficult to justify sending any foreign aid, both among economists and the general populace, regardless of Jamaica's past ties, and especially when considering current market volatility. However, Jamaica is a valuable local ally; losing them would be significant. The costs are also fairly low, and the benefits of a bailout could greatly boost our international image, especially if the United States turns to austerity.
strings.JAM_flavor.79.a: Bail them out, but make sure our companies can fend off these gangsters if necessary.
strings.JAM_News.5.t: {get_newspaper_header}Jamaica Declares Independence from Britain, Bustamante Declared President
strings.JAM_News.5.desc:
Following the mass riots in Kingston, Prime Minister Bustamante has cemented his rule in Jamaica, a task he's undertaken since he first took office years ago. Declaring full independence from Britain and declaring Jamaica a republic, with himself as its president, replacing the governor general. A protégé of Bustamante, Donald Sangster, has taken up the role of Prime Minister.

With Jamaica now breaking off from the OFN, Jamaica has found a new ally with the Iberian Union. After stating in an address that the Kingston Riots were “spurred on by Washington in an attempt to overthrow the government,” Bustamante was photographed with Iberian diplomats visiting the King's House, the newly declared presidential home. When asked for comment, officials from Washington 'are saddened to see Jamaica side with authoritarianism.'
strings.JAM_News.5.a: I think Mr. Seaga will be interested in hearing our “concerns” on this matter.
strings.JAM_News.5.c: From one colonial master to another.
strings.JAM_News.11.desc:
Faced with a hurricane, nationwide blackouts from the Oil Crisis, rumors of a failed coup during the storm, and mass gang violence, the JLP has been hammered yet again with the sudden death of Prime Minister Donald Sangster. The mounting crisis has caused new Prime Minister Hugh Shearer to make a public address calling for civility and reconciliation between the militant factions of Jamaica.

The Iberian Union has sent aid to the island, reaffirming their relationship despite the disaster. President Bustamante has been notable absent during the crisis, with reports of his health declining. Shearer now faces the risk of losing another public figure to shore up his diminishing government.
strings.JAM_News.11.a: How can so much go so wrong so fast?
strings.JAM_News.12.t: {get_newspaper_header}Pro-American Coup in Jamaica Amidst Nationwide Blackout
strings.JAM_News.12.desc:
Faced with a hurricane, nationwide blackouts from the Oil Crisis, mass gang violence, and the sudden death of Prime Minister Donald Sangster by heart attack the JLP regime has been overthrown by the Jamaican Labour Party. The coup's leader, a prominent JLP member named Edward Seaga, has announced “a new era of liberalism, dignity and safety,” in his first public address to the nation.

Regional experts fear that Seaga will be just as authoritative as Bustamante, with the only difference being his American backing instead of an Iberian one. President Bustamante remains President, but is under house arrest and has made no comment on the unraveling political situation.
strings.JAM_News.12.b: We had a good thing going there...
strings.JAM_News.18.t: {get_newspaper_header}Left Wing PNP Claims Victory in Jamaican Elections
strings.JAM_News.18.desc:
Once more, the People's National Party was proclaimed victorious in recently held elections, retaining the helm it has held over the Republic of Jamaica since the island earned its independence five years prior and entrenching its Democratic Socialist course.

This outcome is bound to further infuriate those opposing the young nation's recent economic reforms, which reelected leader Michael Manley has confirmed he had no intention to stall, despite facing significant strain in the aftermath of the Oil Crisis.

In a context of growing protests and rising political violence, exacerbated by street gangs in loose association with the ruling party, many observers fear that the Prime Minister's hasty populist policies will soon take their toll on the country's prospects for long-term stability.
strings.JAM_News.18.a: Bustamante's legacy has finally been extinguished.
strings.JAM_News.18.b: “Damn it Seaga - This was our only shot!”
strings.JAM_News.18.c: Trying too much, and too soon.
strings.JAM_News.19.t: {get_newspaper_header}Right Wing Returns to Power in Jamaica in Surprise Victory
strings.JAM_News.19.desc:
In a surprising turn, Michael Manley of the People's National Party failed to secure reelection, conceding the nation's leadership to the Jamaican Labour Party's Edward Seaga. While many have attributed this outcome to rising political violence and economic strain in the aftermath of the Oil Crisis, several PNP figures voiced claims of foreign influence and electoral meddling.

A music producer and company owner of West Indies Records Limited, the Prime Minister-elect comes as an unusual newcomer in the Jamaican political scene. Marking a notable distancing of the party from its previous Bustamante-era platform, Seaga has confirmed his intent to steer the country toward a more pro-American position, while maintaining ongoing diplomatic ties with the Veracruz Pact. However, the JLP's narrow majority and its contested legitimacy might prove an additional challenge to future governance.
strings.JAM_News.19.a: Just when you thought you got rid of them.
strings.JAM_News.19.b: “Get the prime minister elect on the line, I want to congratulate him personally.”
strings.JAM_News.19.c: A fresh face bearing Uncle Sam's shadow.
strings.JAM_News.20.desc:
Richard Hart of the People's Freedom Movement claims victory in the recently held Jamaican snap elections, following the collapse of the ruling coalition formed between his group and the now rivaling People's National Party.

The newly elected leader blamed American involvement while addressing the current economic and political struggles plaguing the nation, even going as far as to claim his opponent Michael Manley was nothing more than a “puppet” to Washington's interests.

This outcome is bound to further degrade the already frigid diplomatic ties between the island and the United States, with Hart promising much more aggressive nationalization policies and a firmer stance against what he considers attempts at “bourgeois subversion”.
strings.JAM_News.21.desc:
Following the collapse of the PFM-PNP coalition, Richard Hart of the PFP, a splinter party from the PNP, has managed to win the snap election by a narrow margin. As Hart largely maintains a socialist approach, like his predecessor, in domestic decision-making, his foreign policy is marked by a staunch, populist anti-Americanism, pointing the source of Jamaica's current woes to Washington's meddlings.

Hart has accused the former Prime Minister Michael Manley to have been under the sway of American intelligence agencies while criticizing him for inaction on social matters. He vows to expand the ongoing nationalization programs while creating a sustainable welfare state. Although his dedication to social justice has won over many voters, some worry that his antagonism may isolate Jamaica from one of her most important benefactors.
strings.JAM_News.21.a: We'll keep the red flag flying here.
strings.JAM_News.22.t: {get_newspaper_header}Jamaican Popular Republic Declares Emergency Following Canadian Skirmish
strings.JAM_News.22.desc:
In response to increasingly fierce military clashes between the Jamaican Popular Republic and Canadian authorities, the rogue government helmed by former Royal Air Force pilot William Strachan has established a state of emergency. According to local reports, the announcement correlates with a significant uptick in repressive crackdowns against the dissent sparked by the recent crisis.

These events follow the island's earlier declaration of independence after the collapse of negotiations over the West Indies Federation proposal. The act, as well as the state's sweeping new collectivisation policies, has earned firm condemnation from Washington officials, while Strachan has declared the situation as only being the result of attempts at US subversion.
strings.JAM_News.23.desc:
Earlier today, left-wing representatives from all across the West Indies assembled in Kingston to join under the first All-Caribbean People's Conference.

Invited at the behest of Jamaican leader William Strachan, many socialist and even pan-African movements were given a platform to share their grievances and voice their support for revolutionary causes both near and worldwide.

As the conference concluded, the most recurring issues were calls for a drastic end to acts of “British imperialism” across the region, and a shared hope for closer cooperative bonds among the young island-nations.
strings.JAM_News.24.desc:
The transitional Prime Minister of the Jamaican Popular Republic, Billy Strachan, has stepped down from his position following the government's full reorganization. With Bustamante's Jamaican Labour Party banned from participation and its membership split into successor parties, a coalition government was formed between the social-democratic People's National Party and the socialist People's Freedom Movement. Richard Hart, a former PNP member and a communist, has been chosen as the new Prime Minister.

As a longtime friend of Strachan, Hart upholds similar principles of egalitarianism and workers' solidarity—having been one of the few expelled from the PNP in the '50s for his self-declared Marxist views. Although he now has to work with the same party that rejected him years ago, Hart declares it to be “just what it takes to rebuild a democracy.”
strings.JAM_News.24.a: I really wish Busta was still here.
strings.JAM_News.24.b: Good or bad, at least it is not Busta.
